title: Chapter IV
focus: obsession and the discovery of life

teacherSummary.text: Victor works tirelessly, masters chemistry, and discovers the cause of life. Gathering materials from charnel houses and dissecting rooms, he neglects family and health for nearly two years as he builds a being of gigantic stature.

vocabulary.definition: To put off till to-morrow, or from day to day
vocabulary.context: I wished, as it were, to procrastinate all that related to my feelings of affection until the great object, which swallowed up every habit of my nature, should be completed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “procrastinate”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A house where beasts are butchered for the market
vocabulary.context: The dissecting room and the slaughterhouse furnished many of my materials; and often did my human nature turn with loathing from my occupation, whilst, still urged on by an eagerness which perpetually increased, I brought my work near to a conclusion.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “slaughterhouse”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Dividing or separating the parts of an animal or vegetable body
vocabulary.context: The dissecting room and the slaughterhouse furnished many of my materials; and often did my human nature turn with loathing from my occupation, whilst, still urged on by an eagerness which perpetually increased, I brought my work near to a conclusion.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dissecting”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To wet by little dips or strokes
vocabulary.context: Who shall conceive the horrors of my secret toil, as I dabbled among the unhallowed damps of the grave, or tortured the living animal to animate the lifeless clay?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dabble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Containing the bodies of the dead
vocabulary.context: Now I was led to examine the cause and progress of this decay, and forced to spend days and nights in vaults and charnel-houses.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “charnel”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: I knew my silence disquieted them; and I well remembered the words of my father: “I know that while you are pleased with yourself, you will think of us with affection, and we shall hear regularly from you.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disquiet”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Concealed or hidden out of the way
vocabulary.context: In a thousand ways he smoothed for me the path of knowledge, and made the most abstruse enquiries clear and facile to my apprehension.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “abstruse”: ab- (Latin ab, "away from"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I will not lead you on, unguarded and ardent as I then was, to your destruction and infallible misery.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unguard”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The produce of the vine for one season, in grapes or in wine
vocabulary.context: It was a most beautiful season; never did the fields bestow a more plentiful harvest, or the vines yield a more luxuriant vintage: but my eyes were insensible to the charms of nature.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “vintage”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The science which treats of the phenomena of living organisms
vocabulary.context: I revolved these circumstances in my mind, and determined thenceforth to apply myself more particularly to those branches of natural philosophy which relate to physiology.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “physiology”: log (Greek logos, "word, reason"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Body-snatching to supply anatomy schools was a real scandal of the era. 'Natural philosophy' was the period term for science.

significance: Victor withholds the secret from Walton, warning 'how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge'—the novel's core moral caution.
discussionQuestions: Victor refuses to tell Walton how he created life. Why is this choice important?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

options: The cause of generation and life

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter IV,” how does Shelley show obsession and the discovery of life? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter IV, how does Shelley develop the idea of obsession and the discovery of life? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter IV develops the idea of obsession and the discovery of life. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter IV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of obsession and the discovery of life. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter IV suggests about obsession and the discovery of life. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and tone / mood), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter IV to complicate the reader's understanding of obsession and the discovery of life. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter IV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of obsession and the discovery of life responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter IV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of obsession and the discovery of life follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter IV and its treatment of obsession and the discovery of life. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and tone / mood, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter IV as evidence for a larger claim about obsession and the discovery of life in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter IV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of obsession and the discovery of life. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

options: The produce of the vine for one season, in grapes or in wine
The science which treats of the phenomena of living organisms

satQuestions.passage: I see by your eagerness, and the wonder and hope which your eyes express, my friend, that you expect to be informed of the secret with which I am acquainted; that cannot be: listen patiently until the end of my story, and you will easily perceive why I am reserved upon that subject. I will not lead you on, unguarded and ardent as I then was, to your destruction and infallible misery. Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge, and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter IV”?
options: Obsession and the discovery of life

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Victor refuses to tell Walton how he created life. Why is this choice important? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are procrastinate, slaughterhouse, dissecting, dabbled, charnel. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “I wished, as it were, to procrastinate all that related to my feelings of affection until the great object, which swallowed up every habit of my nature, should be completed.” Webster's says: To put off till to-morrow, or from day to day. Now the word history: “procrastinate”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “slaughterhouse”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “dissecting”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Body-snatching to supply anatomy schools was a real scandal of the era. 'Natural philosophy' was the period term for science. Why does this chapter matter? Victor withholds the secret from Walton, warning 'how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge'—the novel's core moral caution. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see foreshadowing, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to obsession and the discovery of life.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Tone / mood, Imagery.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: I see by your eagerness, and the wonder and hope which your eyes express, my friend, that you expect to be informed of the secret with which I am acquainted; that cannot be: listen patiently until the end of my story, and you will easily perceive why I am reserved upon that subject. I will not lead you on, unguarded and ardent as I then was, to your destruction and infallible misery. Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge, and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Tone / mood, Imagery: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter IV,” how does Shelley show obsession and the discovery of life? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about obsession and the discovery of life, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes obsession and the discovery of life. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
